title: My Son's First Buck Hunt Gave Me a Memory I'll Never Forget - 97.9 WGRD
content: If you're a deer hunter, you never forget the feeling of harvesting your first deer. Watching my son experience the excitement of harvesting his first buck with a bow is a memory we'll cherish for the rest of our lives. My son's first word wasn't Mom or Dad. It was "Buck." I used to hold him up in front of one of my deer mounts, point to it, say 'buck,' and let him reach out and touch it. Then one day, he said it himself. From that moment on, I knew something special was beginning. Passing along what I've learned and sharing my passion with the next generation has turned into an incredible journey that we'll cherish forever. I remember getting Evan his first bow and setting up a little shooting range in our old barn. I also remember the times he'd sit in the blind with me, watching deer and taking in all the amazing things Mother Nature had to offer. Long before he was old enough to sit in a stand on his own, he was already learning, observing, and sharing those special moments with me. It's been such a blessing to share these experiences with Evan and his brother and watch them grow into the fine young outdoorsmen they are today. This past weekend, it all came full circle for the three of us when Evan harvested his very first buck with his bow. It's a moment we'll never forget and one that makes all those years of memories together even more special. Read More: 10 Michigan Deer Season Safety Tips Every Hunter Needs My sons and I have spent years shooting our bows together, putting in countless hours practicing in the barn and from our tree stands. It's pretty special to see all that practice finally pay off. My favorite time of year is always from Halloween until the day before gun season. The deer are moving, and those big bucks we've been watching on our trail cameras start showing up. There's just something about this time of year that makes it so special. Evan's big brother, Isaak, spotted the buck coming into the field and watched as it walked straight toward his little brother. Evan didn't even realize the buck was there until it approached and started feeding in the food plot. Evan said, "My legs started shaking, my arms were shaking, and I could barely lift my bow. Then, just like that, one, two, three seconds later, I let my arrow fly. I couldn't believe how fast it all happened!" Isaak said he heard the shot, followed by the crash, and immediately made his way over to see what had happened. He said, "Evan couldn't even get any words out. He was just holding his hands up, saying, 'Big buck!'" I heard the shot too, but I was surrounded by deer and couldn't move. Once the area cleared, I made my way down to the boys, only to find out they had already tracked the deer themselves, something I've spent years teaching both of them. Inside, I was pretty choked up inside, but I had to play it cool and let the boys tell me everything that had just happened. It was one of those moments I'll never forget. This was a Hall of Fame weekend for the boys and me. I couldn't be prouder of both of them for their hard work, patience, and willingness to wait for the right deer. These are the kinds of memories the three of us will be talking about for the rest of our lives. It doesn't get any better than this, and it doesn't get much more "Pure Michigan" than that! Now it's Isaak's and my turn to hopefully get our chance at bringing home a big buck or doe. The memories keep coming, and we're looking forward to seeing what the rest of the season has in store. 👇BELOW: 2025 Michigan Deer Season All Seasons Harvest Report👇

title: What Is Going on With Taiwan Semiconductor Stock on Monday? - TradingView
content: Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. Ltd. TSM stock rose almost 4% Monday as chip stocks rebounded and investors weighed reports that the chipmaker is considering an expansion into advanced memory production. The SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust was up about 1.7%. The potential move could broaden TSMC’s role in the AI hardware supply chain beyond its core logic-chip manufacturing business. TSMC is evaluating plans to produce 3D DRAM at the request of NVIDIA Corp. NVDA, its largest customer, The Information reported on Friday. The move would give TSMC exposure to another part of the AI hardware market at a time when demand for advanced memory remains elevated. The contract chipmaker could either build new factories dedicated to advanced memory or acquire and convert an existing facility, Reuters reported Friday. The reported plans would place TSMC in competition with established memory suppliers including Samsung Electronics Co. Ltd. SSNLF, SK Hynix Inc. SKHY and Micron Technology Inc. MU. For TSMC, the initiative would extend its involvement in AI infrastructure beyond manufacturing advanced logic chips for customers such as NVIDIA. Despite Monday’s gain, TSM remains below several major moving averages. The stock trades about 6% below its 20-day simple moving average (SMA), about 10% below its 50-day SMA and about 3% below its 200-day SMA. The 20-day SMA also remains below the 50-day SMA, keeping the near-term technical trend under pressure. TSMC carries a Buy consensus rating with an average price forecast of $559.38. Recent actions include Bernstein maintaining Outperform while raising its target to $600 on Nov. 4, Barclays maintaining Overweight while raising its target to $670 on Oct. 16, and DA Davidson maintaining Buy with a $500 target on Oct. 16. TSMC carries a 9.32% weighting in the VanEck Semiconductor ETF, 6.28% in the Franklin Income Focus ETF and 7.32% in the Brown Advisory Flexible Equity ETF. Shares of Samsung and SK Hynix in Seoul gave up their gains from earlier in the day but still ended up 0.6% and 0.4% higher. To be sure, SK Hynix’s U.S. stock SKHY, and TSM were down 3.5% and 0.3% respectively in overnight trading. Among the key triggers on Monday was the controversy engulfing Nvidia. Over the weekend, CEO Jensen Huang admitted to having an affair with a person U.S. authorities suspect to be a Chinese spy. Nvidia said it launched an investigation into the issues, even as analysts debated the potential fallout. NVDA stock plunged 5.7% in overnight trading ahead of Monday. Some analysts believe that the incident could have far reaching consequences, including a near-term overhang on NVDA stock and Huang ultimately losing his CEO title. South Korean chip stocks were hit by the global sell-off in AI and semiconductor shares last week. Investors worried that a new U.S. Congress could impose tighter rules on AI data-center construction, potentially slowing the buildout and weakening future demand for the memory chips that Samsung and SK Hynix supply. The selling then fed on itself: overseas investors pulled money from the market, and Samsung and SK Hynix – two of the KOSPI’s biggest stocks – took the brunt. By the week’s close on Nov. 6, the KOSPI had fallen about 11.7%. Investors are expected to closely track updates around the Nvidia controversy, including a potential congressional investigation. title: TSM Stock at 21x After a 30% Chip Sell-Off [2026] - shattered.io
content: Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing, the company behind the NYSE ticker TSM, is the stock a Motley Fool columnist would buy and hold after a brutal stretch for chip shares. In a column syndicated on Yahoo Finance and headlined “Not Nvidia. Not Micron. After the Chip Sell-Off, I’d Buy This AI Stock and Hold It Forever.”, the author argues that TSM stock offers a better deal than the two names that dominated the AI trade. Listings show the piece ran on November 7, 2026. The timing matters. The PHLX Semiconductor Sector index sits roughly 30% below where it stood on October 6, Nvidia is down 21%, and Micron is down 34%. TSMC trades near 21 times forward earnings, while Micron changes hands at about 4 times. Compare that to Apple’s 36x forward earnings, and a 21x multiple on the company that builds the world’s most advanced AI processors starts to look like a real debate rather than a throwaway pick. This analysis walks through the numbers behind the call, tests the thesis against the obvious objections, and sorts what is confirmed from what is opinion. Nothing here is investment advice. The “hold it forever” framing belongs to the Motley Fool columnist, and no price target appears in the verified material. The week's biggest stories in tech, gaming and security, in one email. Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions. Start with the damage from the semiconductor sell-off. According to the research behind this story, the PHLX Semiconductor Sector index is down approximately 30% since October 6. That index tracks the biggest US-listed chip designers, equipment makers, and manufacturers, so a drop of that size is a sector-wide event rather than one company’s bad quarter. Nvidia, which trades as NVDA on Nasdaq, fell about 21% from its October 6 record close in the period the column cites. A separate market update put the slide at 21.96%. Micron, ticker MU, took a bigger hit at roughly 34%. TSMC shares finished the referenced week down 7.61%, which is a smaller loss than either of the stocks the columnist passed over. Outlets covering the move frame it as a question of whether the AI buildout can keep its pace. Upside asked whether the good times are over for AI stocks, and our own earlier report on the $2.5 trillion AI sell-off and its four triggers traced how political risk fed the rout. The comparison table later in this piece collects the confirmed figures side by side. The column’s logic is a picks-and-shovels argument. Every company designing an advanced AI accelerator needs someone to manufacture it, and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing is the largest third-party chip foundry on the planet. If Nvidia, AMD, or a hyperscaler’s in-house team wins the next design contest, the wafers still run through TSMC fabs. That structure explains why the columnist treats the foundry as the safer way to own the AI chip stocks theme. A designer can lose share to a rival. A foundry that makes chips for all the rivals collects revenue either way. The column also notes that TSMC’s forward multiple of about 21 sits close to Nvidia’s, so buyers do not pay a steep premium for the lower design risk. Be clear about what this argument is. It is a stock pick from a financial-media columnist, published the day after a sector-wide drop. The Motley Fool is known for long-horizon, buy-and-hold advice, so a “hold forever” label fits the house style. Readers should weigh the reasoning and the data, then decide for themselves whether any of it applies to their own portfolio. The strongest number in the thesis is TSMC’s foundry market share, and it explains most of the column’s confidence. According to the research, the company captures 73% of contract semiconductor-manufacturing spending. Put plainly, of every $100 that chip designers spend to have someone else build their processors, about $73 goes to TSMC. That concentration cuts both ways. For investors it signals pricing power and a customer base that cannot easily switch, because moving a leading-edge design to another fab takes years of engineering work. For the industry it creates a single point of failure. A fab outage, a regional shock, or a trade restriction would ripple through nearly every major AI product at once. The market has priced the dependence in for years, and the semiconductor sell-off did not change it. What changed is the multiple that investors will pay for chip exposure. When the SOX index loses a third of its value from a peak, the question shifts from “who is growing fastest” to “who owns the part of the chain that does not go away.” Beyond that foundry market share, TSMC also serves a second business that gets less attention. Its mature-node fabs, which the company’s earnings materials describe in terms of 180 nm and 90 nm processes, supply power-management chips used in AI data centers. Those parts are cheap next to a flagship accelerator, but a server rack cannot run without them. TSMC backs its position with spending. The company raised its 2026 capital budget to $60 billion to $64 billion, according to its second-quarter 2026 earnings call transcript on the investor relations site. In 2025 the company spent $40.9 billion, and in 2024 it spent $29.8 billion. Run the arithmetic and the scale becomes clear. Capex rose about 37% from 2024 to 2025. The 2026 guidance implies a further jump of roughly 47% at the low end and 56% at the high end versus 2025 (my calculation from the reported figures). Few manufacturers of any kind raise their capital budgets by half in a single year. The earnings call also broke the 2026 budget into buckets. About 70% to 80% goes to advanced process technologies, roughly 10% to specialty technologies, and 10% to 20% to advanced packaging, testing, mask making, and related work. On a $60 billion to $64 billion budget, the advanced-process share alone works out to somewhere between $42 billion and $51 billion (again my arithmetic). Those buckets tell you what management thinks the AI cycle needs. Packaging has become a bottleneck for large accelerators, so the 10% to 20% slice deserves attention. If it grows in later years, it would signal that chip assembly, not wafer starts, limits how fast customers can ship. The valuation gap drives the column’s conclusion. TSMC trades at about 21 times forward earnings, a multiple the article describes as similar to Nvidia’s. Micron trades at roughly 4 times. A five-fold difference between two chip stocks, in the same sell-off, begs an explanation. The usual explanation is cyclicality. Memory makers earn peak profits when prices spike and then watch margins collapse when supply catches up. Investors apply a low multiple to peak-looking earnings because they expect those earnings to fall. A foundry with long-term contracts and 73% of its market looks steadier, so buyers pay more per dollar of profit. The columnist chose not to buy Micron despite the cheap multiple, which signals skepticism about earnings durability. Memory pricing has been wild this year. Our report on DDR5 pricing, where a chip that cost $8.70 now sells for $48, shows how hot the market ran. Micron’s own quote page on Robinhood gives readers a place to check the live numbers. A 4x multiple says the market expects profits to drop. If memory prices hold, Micron looks mispriced. If they roll over, 4x was the right call. The Motley Fool column sided with the safer exposure, and the 34% drop shows many investors share that unease. Management commentary supports the demand story, though readers should remember that executives talk up their own business. During the third-quarter earnings call, TSMC Chairman and CEO C.C. Wei said, “All AI players are working with TSMC,” according to CRN Asia’s coverage of the call. The same report quotes him on supply: “The demand remained far above what the company could currently supply.” Earlier in the year Wei described the long-run trend in similar terms. In July he said, “The CAGR is getting stronger and stronger and stronger,” as The Next Platform reported in a piece about how AI chips now drive around a third of TSMC’s revenue. The quote refers to the compound growth rate in the company’s AI-related business. Nvidia’s Jensen Huang has praised the supply chain in public. In a conversation reported by PJFP alongside Lex Fridman, he said, “Nothing gives me more pleasure than last year when my entire supply chain’s stock price went up 300%, mine stayed flat.” The 300% figure is Huang’s own characterization, and this article has not verified it. The remark still shows how Nvidia’s CEO sees the relative winners in the AI buildout. Taken together, these statements describe a company that says it cannot build enough, which is the best possible message for a foundry. They do not guarantee that customers keep ordering at the same pace if AI budgets shrink. A supply-constrained business can turn into an oversupplied one quickly when end demand cools. The sell-off did not stay inside the GPU and memory names. Chips that serve phones, industrial gear, and data centers all felt pressure from the same risk-off mood. We covered the ripple in several earlier pieces, and they paint a mixed picture of where demand holds and where it fades. Microchip guided its next quarter down 1%, and the company pointed to stretching lead times and foundry pricing, as we reported in Microchip Guides Down 1% as Lead Times Stretch. That is a small number, but it comes from a chip company far from the AI spotlight, and it shows foundry capacity still limits parts of the market. Qualcomm showed the split between mobile weakness and data-center promise. The stock fell 9% as handset revenue dropped 26% to $5.14 billion, with data-center revenue of $650 million offering a counterweight. AI exposure helps, but it does not yet offset a slumping phone business at the scale Qualcomm needs. Arm, which licenses designs rather than building chips, guided its next quarter to $1.54 billion, only just above the $1.53 billion analysts expected. For anyone sorting through AI chip stocks, the pattern is clear: companies with direct, capacity-constrained exposure to AI wafers have the strongest story, and those with consumer-device exposure carry the most doubt. The three stocks in the column represent three different bets on the same boom. Nvidia designs the accelerators, Micron supplies the memory that feeds them, and TSMC manufactures the logic. Each faces a different failure mode, which is why the table below sorts them by what could go wrong. AMD sits in the designer camp as well. Our look at the AMD stress test, with $8.5 billion in data-center revenue out of $13.4 billion total, shows the same dynamic. Whoever wins sockets in the next AI generation, TSMC probably builds the winner, and that structural advantage is what the Motley Fool column rewards. TSMC’s recent history reads like a case study in compounding. The company grew sales 35.9% in 2025, according to the figures cited in the research, while it lifted capex from $29.8 billion to $40.9 billion. Growth that fast, funded by heavy reinvestment, is what pushed AI chip stocks to the highs of early October. The sector has seen similar swings before. Chip stocks tend to sell off sharply when investors question the durability of end demand, and then recover once customers confirm their orders. A semiconductor sell-off of roughly 30% in about a month is large, but the real test is whether capex guidance and customer orders hold, not the stock chart alone. What differs this time is the size of the commitments. Hyperscalers have borrowed heavily to fund data centers, and our report on Big Tech bonds pushing US issuance to a $1.88 trillion record shows how much debt now sits behind the buildout. If those buyers pull back, the foundry feels it first because it must order wafers months ahead. For investors, the rout reset expectations. TSMC now trades near 21 times forward earnings, and Micron trades near 4 times. Those are the clearest signals that the market is separating durable businesses from cyclical ones. For hardware buyers, the effects arrive more slowly. Capacity expansion at TSMC takes years, so a $60 billion to $64 billion budget in 2026 lands in products over the following cycles. If the sell-off prompts customers to trim orders, GPU and memory supply could loosen. If it does not, prices for consumer parts could stay high. Our hardware coverage tracks both sides. Data from market pages such as StockAnalysis lets readers check TSM’s price, valuation, and financial history directly. Checking those pages matters more than trusting any single column, since forward multiples move daily and the figures in this article reflect the Motley Fool’s November 7 snapshot. No stock deserves the word “forever” without a list of what could break it. A column that champions one company after a drop should face the same scrutiny as any bull case. The table below sets out how a bull and a bear would read the same facts. The same 73% share that makes TSMC attractive also makes it a target for policy. Export controls, tariffs, and geopolitical tension affect where the company can build and whom it can sell to. The verified material does not quantify those risks, so this article leaves them as open variables instead of guessing at numbers. Capital intensity adds another weight. Spending $60 billion or more in one year only pays off if fabs stay full. A stock priced at 21 times earnings has less room for error than one priced at 4 times, even though the latter carries more cycle risk. These are analytical judgments, not forecasts from the sources, and none is a recommendation. The takeaway: the Motley Fool column makes a structural case, not a timing call. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing builds the chips for most of the AI industry, holds 73% of contract chipmaking spending, and plans to invest $60 billion to $64 billion this year. After a 30% drop in the SOX index, it trades near 21 times forward earnings. Against that, the bear case is real. The stock is not cheap, spending is enormous, and a single supplier carries enormous weight for the whole sector. Anyone considering TSM stock after the semiconductor sell-off should read the company’s own filings, check live prices, and weigh how much concentration they already hold in AI chip stocks. Which stock does the Motley Fool recommend after the chip sell-off? The column names Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing, which trades as TSM on the NYSE. It positions the stock as a better buy-and-hold choice than Nvidia or Micron. How far have chip stocks fallen? The PHLX Semiconductor Sector index is down approximately 30% since October 6. Nvidia is down 21% and Micron is down 34% over the period the column cites. How is TSM stock valued? The column puts TSMC at about 21 times forward earnings, similar to Nvidia. Micron trades at roughly 4 times. What is TSMC’s foundry market share? TSMC accounts for 73% of contract semiconductor-manufacturing spending, according to the research cited here. How much will TSMC spend on capital projects in 2026? The company guided to $60 billion to $64 billion, up from $40.9 billion in 2025 and $29.8 billion in 2024. Is this investment advice? No. This is news analysis based on a published column and public data. The “hold forever” view belongs to the columnist, and readers should do their own research before buying any stock. Why does Micron trade at only 4 times earnings? The article does not state the market’s reasoning. A common explanation is memory-cycle risk, where profits peak and then fall as supply catches up, but that is analysis rather than a confirmed fact from the column. title: Nickel Asia subsidiaries bag seven awards at inaugural TSM Excellence AwardsNickel Asia subsidiaries bag seven awards at inaugural TSM Excellence Awards - The Manila Times
content: NICKEL Asia Corp. (NAC), through subsidiaries Rio Tuba Nickel Mining Corp. (RTNMC) and Taganito Mining Corp. (TMC), received seven awards at the Philippines’ inaugural Towards Sustainable Mining (TSM) Excellence Awards on Oct. 27 at Conrad Manila. The ceremony was part of the Mining Philippines International Conference and Exhibition organized by the Chamber of Mines of the Philippines (COMP). COMP Chairman Michael Toledo said the awards recognize companies demonstrating responsible mining through their decisions, systems, and standards. The TSM framework recognizes mining companies through independently verified assessments. Scores of 4.5 to 5.0 qualify for gold, while 3.5 to 4.49 earn silver. RTNMC received four gold awards, including Excellence in Community Partnership and Shared Development, Safety Leadership and Zero Harm, and Water Stewardship and Watershed Responsibility. It was also the sole gold recipient in the Cross-Cutting category, the evening’s top award. TMC earned gold in Excellence in Community Partnership and Shared Development, and silver awards in Safety Leadership and Zero Harm and the Cross-Cutting category. NAC Senior Vice President for Sustainability, Risk Management and Corporate Affairs Jose Bayani Baylon said the recognition demonstrates Filipinos’ ability to meet international mining standards, emphasizing the importance of communicating the industry’s responsible practices. The Philippines adopted TSM through COMP in 2017, becoming the first Asian country to implement the internationally recognized sustainability framework.
